Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes: tmux-agent-fleet.

https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet

It is a lightweight tmux plugin that provides a searchable `fzf` command palette across live panes:

- Opens with `prefix + f`
- Detects Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, Fable, shells, and other foreground processes
- Jumps directly to the selected pane
- Shows a live pane preview
- Uses tmux process metadata—no daemon or harness hooks
- Does not inject commands, rename sessions, manage worktrees, or send telemetry
- Can optionally include Agent Deck sessions

Requirements are tmux 3.2+, Bash 4+, and `fzf`:
https://github.com/junegunn/fzf

TPM installation:

```tmux
set -g @plugin 'kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet'
```

Then reload tmux, run `prefix + I`, and open it with `prefix + f`.

One important distinction: it is a switcher and monitor, not an orchestrator. It discovers already-running agents rather than launching or owning them. If you want automatic worktree creation, agent launching, merging, and PR creation, dmux is the heavier alternative:

https://github.com/standardagents/dmux  
https://dmux.ai/

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Yes. I’d assemble this from interoperable components rather than adopt one agent framework end-to-end.

1. Company issue graph

Recommended stack:

- Plane as the human-facing issue/project system of record.
  - Issues, cycles, modules, views, triage, and API.
  - AGPL-3.0.
  - https://github.com/makeplane/plane
  - https://developers.plane.so/api-reference/introduction

- PostgreSQL + Apache AGE as the authoritative graph projection.
  - AGE adds graph storage and Cypher queries to PostgreSQL, avoiding a second operational database.
  - Apache-2.0.
  - https://github.com/apache/age
  - https://age.apache.org/

- Graphiti only for derived temporal/semantic memory.
  - Useful for extracting entities, decisions, and changing relationships from issue comments, run logs, and documents.
  - Do not make LLM-extracted Graphiti edges authoritative; retain provenance back to the original issue, commit, artifact, or message.
  - Apache-2.0.
  - https://github.com/getzep/graphiti
  - https://help.getzep.com/graphiti/getting-started/overview

A practical graph model:

```text
Company → Team → Project → Issue
Issue → PR → Commit
Issue → Run → Artifact
Issue → Decision
Run → Agent
```

Typed edges should include `BLOCKS`, `DUPLICATES`, `IMPLEMENTS`, `CAUSED_BY`, `SUPERSEDES`, `VERIFIED_BY`, and `PRODUCED`. Every derived edge should carry source URL, source revision, extractor version, confidence, and timestamp.

2. Agent harness contracts

Use small public standards at each boundary:

- JSON Schema for your own stable `Task`, `Run`, `Event`, `Artifact`, `Evidence`, and `Review` objects.
  - https://json-schema.org/

- CloudEvents as the event envelope.
  - Gives events standard IDs, source, type, subject, time, and content type.
  - https://cloudevents.io/
  - https://github.com/cloudevents/spec

- MCP for agent-to-tool and agent-to-resource access.
  - Good for issue queries, repository operations, test runners, graph lookups, and artifact retrieval.
  - It is not a complete workflow or agent-to-agent protocol.
  - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest
  - https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/specification

- A2A for remote agent discovery and agent-to-agent task exchange.
  - Use only when agents are independently deployed services; don’t require it for local subprocess workers.
  - Apache-2.0.
  - https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A

- AGENTS.md for repository-local operating instructions.
  - https://agents.md/

- Inspect for reproducible evaluation tasks, solvers, scorers, sandboxes, and logs.
  - Better suited to evaluations than production orchestration.
  - https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/
  - https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai

- OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions for traces and metrics.
  - https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/tree/main/docs/gen-ai

I would define the harness around an append-only event stream:

```text
task.created
run.started
agent.message
tool.requested
tool.completed
artifact.produced
evidence.attached
review.requested
review.resolved
run.completed
run.failed
```

The critical contract is not the prompt. It is the immutable record connecting inputs, tool calls, code revision, artifacts, evidence, reviewer decisions, and final status.

3. Terminal project cockpit

Choose based on the implementation language:

- TypeScript: OpenTUI
  - Modern TypeScript/Zig TUI library; strongest fit when the surrounding product is already TS.
  - MIT.
  - https://github.com/anomalyco/opentui
  - https://opentui.com/

- Go: Bubble Tea
  - Mature Elm-style architecture with a strong component ecosystem.
  - MIT.
  - https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea

- Python: Textual
  - Rich widgets, CSS-like styling, async operation, testing support, and terminal/web targets.
  - MIT.
  - https://github.com/Textualize/textual
  - https://textual.textualize.io/

Useful public UX references:

- Lazygit for pane navigation, contextual commands, and preview/detail transitions:
  https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit

- k9s for live resource tables, drill-down, filtering, logs, command mode, and keyboard discoverability:
  https://github.com/derailed/k9s

Suggested cockpit layout:

```text
┌ Projects / queues ┬ Issue or run graph ┬ Evidence / live output ┐
│ assigned          │ dependencies       │ logs                   │
│ blocked           │ agents and runs    │ diffs                  │
│ awaiting review   │ artifacts          │ tests                  │
│ recently failed   │ provenance         │ reviewer annotations   │
└───────────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘
```

Recommended default combination

- Plane for issue authoring and collaboration
- PostgreSQL + Apache AGE for the authoritative company graph
- Graphiti for optional semantic/temporal enrichment
- JSON Schema + CloudEvents for internal contracts
- MCP for tools/resources
- A2A only across independently deployed agent services
- Inspect for evaluations
- OpenTelemetry for observability
- OpenTUI for a TypeScript terminal cockpit

That creates a replaceable architecture: the graph, harness, agents, and cockpit share contracts without any one agent framework owning the company’s operational data.

results.stdout:
## Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Ready in about 25 minutes; serves 2–3.

### Ingredients

- 8 oz (225 g) pasta
- 8 oz (225 g) mushrooms, sliced
- 3 packed cups (90 g) baby spinach
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tbsp butter
- ½ cup (120 ml) heavy cream or half-and-half
- ½ cup (45 g) grated Parmesan
- ½ tsp Italian seasoning
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: chili flakes, lemon juice, parsley

### Method

1. Cook the pasta in well-salted water until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of pasta water, then drain.
2. Heat the oil and butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms and leave them undisturbed for 2–3 minutes so they brown. Stir and cook for another 3–4 minutes.
3. Add the garlic, Italian seasoning, and a pinch of chili flakes. Cook for 30 seconds.
4. Lower the heat. Stir in the cream, Parmesan, and about ¼ cup of pasta water.
5. Add the spinach and cook until just wilted.
6. Toss in the pasta. Add more pasta water a splash at a time until the sauce is glossy and coats the noodles.
7. Season with salt, pepper, and a small squeeze of lemon.

Tip: For a lighter version, skip the cream and use ½ cup pasta water plus extra Parmesan. For more protein, add white beans, shredded chicken, or Italian sausage.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Here's the landscape of public, open-source tooling in that space. I've grouped it by what the projects actually do, since "multi-agent framework" and "AI SDLC" get used for pretty different things.

## Agent orchestration frameworks (general-purpose)

- **LangGraph** — https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph — graph/state-machine orchestration with checkpointing, human-in-the-loop interrupts, and durable resume. The most common substrate for building your own SDLC agents.
- **Microsoft Agent Framework** — https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework — the merged successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel; multi-agent conversation patterns plus workflow graphs. (AutoGen itself: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen)
- **CrewAI** — https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI — role-based crews with sequential/hierarchical processes; popular for "planner → coder → reviewer" setups.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python — lightweight handoffs, guardrails, built-in tracing.
- **Claude Agent SDK** — https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python — subagents, hooks, MCP tool loading; what Claude Code itself is built on.
- **MetaGPT** — https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT — the canonical "software company as multi-agent system" (PM/architect/engineer roles emitting SOPs and design docs).
- **ChatDev** — https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev — similar research lineage, waterfall-shaped agent teams.

## Autonomous coding agents you can actually run on a repo

- **OpenHands** (formerly OpenDevin) — https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands — sandboxed agent with shell, browser, and editor; the most mature open-source "resolve this issue" agent.
- **SWE-agent** — https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent — Princeton's agent-computer-interface work; the reference implementation for benchmark-driven issue fixing.
- **Aider** — https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider — repo-map-aware pair programming, strong git-commit discipline per change.
- **Goose** — https://github.com/block/goose — Block's local extensible agent, MCP-native.
- **OpenAI Codex CLI** — https://github.com/openai/codex — and **Gemini CLI** — https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli — both open-source terminal agents.

## The "evidence-based shipping" part

This is where the honest answer diverges from the marketing: **I'm not aware of a single open-source framework that ships evidence-based delivery as its headline product.** What exists is the raw material, and teams assemble it:

- **SWE-bench** — https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench — and **SWE-bench Verified** / **Multimodal**; the standard for "did the patch actually fix the issue," graded by real test suites rather than model judgment.
- **Terminal-Bench** — https://github.com/laude-institute/terminal-bench — agentic terminal tasks with executable verification.
- **SWE-Lancer** — https://github.com/openai/SWELancer-Benchmark — OpenAI's economically-grounded task set with end-to-end tests.
- **Anthropic petri** — https://github.com/safety-research/petri — open-source automated auditing/eval harness.
- **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions** — https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/tree/main/docs/gen-ai — the emerging vendor-neutral standard for agent trace evidence. Backed by **Langfuse** (https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse, self-hostable) and **Arize Phoenix** (https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix) for trace + eval storage.
- **SLSA** / **Sigstore** — https://slsa.dev, https://github.com/sigstore/cosign — provenance attestation. If you want "evidence-based shipping" in the supply-chain sense, an agent-produced build signed with in-toto attestations is the concrete version of that claim.
- **MCP** — https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol — the interop layer letting all of the above share tools.

## Practical recommendation

If you're building this rather than shopping: **LangGraph or Claude Agent SDK for orchestration + OpenHands as the execution sandbox + Langfuse for traces + a real test suite as the gate**, with SWE-bench-style pass/fail as your acceptance signal instead of an LLM judge. The differentiating work is almost entirely in the verification harness, not the orchestration layer — orchestration is close to commoditized now, and the projects that claim otherwise usually don't publish reproducible evidence.

One caveat: this space moves fast enough that my knowledge has a cutoff, so if a specific project matters for a decision, check its repo activity before committing. Want me to search for recent entrants, or go deeper on the verification/attestation side?

I couldn't verify against live sources — the WebSearch permission wasn't granted, so this is from public knowledge as of my cutoff. Worth re-checking the repos, since this space moves fast.

**Short answer: not exactly.** I don't know of a tool that is simultaneously (a) a command-palette UX, (b) daemonless, and (c) harness-neutral. The closest things each drop one leg:

- **claude-squad** — https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad — the nearest fit. A single Go binary TUI that spawns each agent in its own tmux session + git worktree, and is explicitly harness-neutral (Claude Code, Aider, Codex, Gemini, or any command via `-p`). No background daemon: state lives in a local file, tmux holds the processes, so killing the TUI leaves the panes running. But the UX is a list/pane view, not a fuzzy command palette.
- **uzi** — https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi — CLI-first (`uzi prompt`, `uzi ls`, `uzi checkpoint`) for fanning N agents across worktrees + tmux. Daemonless and agent-agnostic, but it's a verb-based CLI with no palette layer.
- **sesh** — https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh — gives you exactly the palette ergonomics (fzf-driven tmux session switcher, configurable startup commands) and is fully daemonless, but knows nothing about agents. Pairing `sesh` with per-agent startup commands is the most common DIY version of what you're describing.
- **vibe-kanban** (https://github.com/BloopAI/vibe-kanban) and **crystal** (https://github.com/stravu/crystal) are harness-neutral and have good UX, but both run a server/Electron process — they fail the zero-daemon test and don't use tmux.

If you want the real thing, the assembly is small: `sesh`/`fzf` for the palette, `git worktree add` per task, `tmux new-session -d` per agent, and a `tmux list-panes -F` + `capture-pane` poll for status. That's roughly what claude-squad is, minus the fuzzy finder — so forking its session layer and bolting `fzf` on the front is probably less work than starting clean.

**Short answer:** I'm not aware of a public, playable demo of a digital twin for a *multi-floor racket sports facility* specifically. Nothing in that niche has the kind of open demo you can click into. The closest public material splits into four adjacent buckets.

**1. Venue/stadium twins (right domain, wrong granularity)**
- **Willow (WillowTwin)** — building-operations twins, and sports venues are one of their marketed verticals (Australian stadiums in particular). Marketing videos, not open demos. https://www.willowinc.com
- **Bentley iTwin** — infrastructure twin platform with a real developer sandbox and sample apps you can run. https://www.bentley.com/software/itwin/ and https://github.com/iTwin/itwinjs-core
- **Matterport** — the largest body of *public, clickable* multi-floor spatial twins, including gyms and venues. Weak on live telemetry, strong on the "walk the building" part. https://matterport.com

**2. Simulation-grade twins you can actually download**
- **NVIDIA Omniverse / Isaac Sim** warehouse and smart-spaces reference scenes are the best public starting point for an *autonomous facility* twin — multi-camera occupancy, agent routing, sensor fusion — even though the sample building is a warehouse, not a padel club. https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/sim and https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse
- **NVIDIA Metropolis** covers the vision-analytics half (people counting, dwell time, zone occupancy). https://developer.nvidia.com/metropolis

**3. Multi-floor indoor mapping (the layer most racket-club twins actually need)**
- **Mappedin** — public multi-level indoor map demos and an SDK; floor-switching, wayfinding, per-space metadata. https://mappedin.com and https://developer.mappedin.com
- **CesiumJS** — open source, good for georeferenced 3D building tiles if you want the twin in a browser. https://cesium.com/platform/cesiumjs/

**4. Autonomous racket-sports operations (real, but not twins)**
This is where the racket-sports world has actually shipped. Unstaffed clubs with app-based door access, lighting, and court booking are standard in Nordic padel/tennis — **Playtomic** (https://playtomic.io) and **MATCHi** (https://www.matchi.se) are the booking/access backbones. Court-level autonomy is **PlaySight** (https://playsight.com) and **Pixellot** (https://www.pixellot.tv) for auto-produced camera coverage, and **Hawk-Eye** (https://www.hawkeyeinnovations.com) at the pro end. None of these expose a spatial twin — they're operational systems with the telemetry a twin would consume.

**The gap, concretely:** the pieces exist separately — occupancy sensing, booking state, court cameras, multi-floor indoor geometry — but I know of no public demo that binds them into one twin for a vertically stacked racket facility. If you're building toward that, the cheapest credible demo is a Mappedin or Cesium multi-floor base layer driven by mock Playtomic-shaped booking/occupancy events, with Omniverse reserved for the point where you need physics or camera simulation rather than a dashboard.

Worth re-checking with live search: whether Willow or Johnson Controls (OpenBlue) has published a racket/multi-sport venue case study since my last reliable information, and whether any of the large European padel chains have shown twin-style facility dashboards publicly.

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
Web search wasn't authorized in this session, so this is from public knowledge — worth verifying the repo links are still active.

**Short answer: there's no off-the-shelf hosted product that does exactly this.** The existing "GitHub profile stats" generators all key off repo *ownership* or *stars*, which is why they leak forks and bookmarks. The authored-commits filter has to come from the contributions API, and then you render it statically yourself.

## The one API that actually gives you "authored commits only"

GitHub's GraphQL `contributionsCollection.commitContributionsByRepository` returns exactly the set you want: repos the user pushed commits to, in a time window. Stars, watch-only repos, and forks you never committed to simply don't appear.

- https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#contributionscollection

Caveats worth knowing before you build on it: it's capped at one year per query (loop year-by-year for a full history), it counts commits attributed to your linked emails, and private-repo contributions require a token with the right scope plus the "include private contributions" profile setting.

The REST alternative is commit search, `q=author:USER`, which is more literal but rate-limited hard and paginates poorly for a full backfill:
- https://docs.github.com/en/rest/search/search#search-commits

## Existing tools, and where each falls short

- **simonw/github-to-sqlite** — https://github.com/simonw/github-to-sqlite — closest thing to a real build log. Fetches repos/commits/releases into SQLite; pair with Datasette (https://datasette.io) and publish the DB. You still write the "authored only" filter as a SQL view, but you get durable history instead of a live API call.
- **lowlighter/metrics** — https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics — renders static SVG via GitHub Actions, has plugins that read contribution data and options to skip forks. Good if you want a rendered card rather than a browsable log.
- **anuraghazra/github-readme-stats** — https://github.com/anuraghazra/github-readme-stats — popular but it's a live-rendering service, not static, and its repo lists are star/ownership-based with manual `exclude_repo=` hacks.

## The pattern you're describing

There isn't an established convention that pairs `llms.txt` with a JSON project manifest. What exists is two separate things people bolt together:

**1. `llms.txt`** — Jeremy Howard's proposal (Sept 2024): a Markdown file at `/llms.txt` with an H1, a blockquote summary, and link sections pointing to clean `.md` versions of pages. Spec and rationale: https://llmstxt.org/ — repo at https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt. A community directory of adopters: https://llmstxt.site/ and https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/. Both directories are dominated by dev-tool docs (Anthropic, Cloudflare, Svelte, Zapier), not personal portfolios — that's the honest answer to "who's doing this."

**2. A JSON manifest of projects** — no standard. The closest real specs are:
- **Schema.org JSON-LD** (`Person` + `CreativeWork`/`SoftwareSourceCode`), embedded as `<script type="application/ld+json">`: https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode. This is what actually gets consumed by crawlers today.
- **JSON Resume** — an established open schema for the résumé half of a portfolio, with a `projects` array: https://jsonresume.org/schema/, repo https://github.com/jsonresume/resume-schema.
- **`.well-known/` URIs** if you want an agent-discoverable path: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8615.html

## What I'd actually recommend

Rather than invent a bespoke `projects.json`, ship three files that each have a real consumer:

- `/llms.txt` — human-written Markdown index linking to `/projects/foo.md` plaintext versions. Per spec, also serve `page.html.md` variants.
- JSON-LD `Person` + `hasPart` array of `SoftwareSourceCode` in your HTML head — this is the one search/AI crawlers already parse.
- `/resume.json` (JSON Resume schema) — gives you a documented, versioned schema for the project list instead of a private one, and there's tooling that renders it.

If you want a bespoke manifest anyway, link it *from* `llms.txt` and give it a `$schema` field pointing at a hosted JSON Schema, so an agent can self-describe it.

One caveat on the premise: agents mostly don't fetch `llms.txt` on their own — there's no widespread crawler support, and the major AI companies haven't committed to it. It's cheap to add and reads well to a human evaluating you, but don't expect it to be the retrieval path. JSON-LD and clean semantic HTML do more work.

If you re-run this with web permissions granted I can pull live examples of portfolios actually shipping both files.

Here's what I'd reach for in each of the three areas, all public/OSS.

## 1. Company issue graph
The pattern that works: ingest issues/PRs/people into a graph store, query it, render it.

- **Ingestion** — [github.com/cli/cli](https://github.com/cli/cli) (`gh api graphql`) for GitHub; GitHub's own GraphQL schema already models issue↔PR↔project↔actor edges, so you often don't need a separate ETL. For Linear, [github.com/linear/linear](https://github.com/linear/linear) (SDK + GraphQL API). For Jira, [github.com/atlassian-api/atlassian-python-api](https://github.com/atlassian-api/atlassian-python-api).
- **Graph store** — [github.com/kuzudb/kuzu](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu) is the strongest fit: embedded (single file, like SQLite), Cypher, columnar, fast for this scale. Alternatives: [github.com/memgraph/memgraph](https://github.com/memgraph/memgraph) (in-memory, Cypher, Bolt), [github.com/apache/age](https://github.com/apache/age) if you're already on Postgres, [github.com/oxigraph/oxigraph](https://github.com/oxigraph/oxigraph) if you want RDF/SPARQL.
- **Rendering** — [github.com/vasturiano/force-graph](https://github.com/vasturiano/force-graph) and its 3D sibling `3d-force-graph` for web; [github.com/cytoscape/cytoscape.js](https://github.com/cytoscape/cytoscape.js) if you need real layout algorithms and graph analysis in the browser; [github.com/sigmajs/sigma.js](https://github.com/sigmajs/sigma.js) (with [graphology](https://github.com/graphology/graphology)) for large node counts via WebGL.
- **Worth stealing from** — [github.com/all-contributors](https://github.com/all-contributors) and [github.com/chaoss/augur](https://github.com/chaoss/augur); Augur (CHAOSS project) is a full open-source repo-health data warehouse and has already solved a lot of the "identity resolution across GitHub/email/commits" problem, which is the actual hard part of a company issue graph.

## 2. Agent harness contracts
Interop specs and typed-contract libraries rather than frameworks:

- **[Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)** — [github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol) for the spec, plus the TS/Python SDKs. This is the tool/resource/prompt contract layer; if you're defining what an agent may touch, define it here.
- **[github.com/a2aproject/A2A](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A)** — Agent2Agent protocol (Linux Foundation), for agent↔agent contracts: agent cards, task lifecycle, capability advertisement. Complementary to MCP, not competing.
- **[github.com/agentcontrolplane](https://github.com/humanlayer/humanlayer)** — HumanLayer, for the approval/human-in-the-loop contract when an agent wants to do something outward-facing.
- **Typed I/O** — [github.com/BoundaryML/baml](https://github.com/BoundaryML/baml) is the best public answer for "the contract between prompt and struct": schema-first, generates typed clients, handles retries on parse failure. [github.com/jxnl/instructor](https://github.com/jxnl/instructor) and [github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai) are lighter-weight variants.
- **Eval/regression contracts** — [github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo](https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo) and [github.com/openai/evals](https://github.com/openai/evals); [github.com/langfuse/langfuse](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse) for tracing what the harness actually did.

## 3. Terminal project cockpit
- **[github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit)** — the reference implementation for this genre; also `lazydocker`. Read its panel/keybinding model before designing your own.
- **[github.com/derailed/k9s](https://github.com/derailed/k9s)** — the other reference; nails "live resource list → drill in → act".
- **Build it on** — [github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea) + [lipgloss](https://github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss) + [bubbles](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles) (Go, Elm architecture) or [github.com/ratatui/ratatui](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui) (Rust). Python: [github.com/Textualize/textual](https://github.com/Textualize/textual), which also gives you a web-served version of the same app for free.
- **Multiplexing / layout** — [github.com/zellij-org/zellij](https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij) has a plugin API and layout files, so a "cockpit" can be a declarative Zellij layout plus a few panes rather than a bespoke TUI. Cheaper path if your panels are mostly other people's CLIs.
- **Panels worth wiring in** — [github.com/dundee/gdu](https://github.com/dundee/gdu), [github.com/ClementTsang/bottom](https://github.com/ClementTsang/bottom), [github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash](https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash) (PR/issue dashboard in the terminal — this is the piece that connects directly to your issue graph).

**How they compose:** Augur or a `gh api graphql` script fills Kuzu; the cockpit is a Bubbletea/Ratatui app whose panels are Cypher queries against that file; MCP exposes the same queries as tools so an agent reads the graph through the identical contract the humans do. That last bit is the actual payoff — one query layer, two consumers.

One caveat worth stating up front: identity resolution (same human across GitHub handle, commit email, Jira account) is where these projects usually stall, and none of the above solves it for you outside Augur's partial approach. Budget for it explicitly.

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
Here's a solid one — mushroom spinach pasta with garlic and parmesan, about 25 minutes.

**Ingredients (serves 3–4)**
- 12 oz pasta (rigatoni, fettuccine, or orecchiette)
- 1 lb mushrooms (cremini/baby bella), sliced
- 5 oz baby spinach
- 4 cloves garlic, minced
- 3 tbsp olive oil + 2 tbsp butter
- 1/2 cup dry white wine (or splash of pasta water + squeeze of lemon)
- 1/2 cup heavy cream (optional but good)
- 3/4 cup grated parmesan
- Salt, black pepper, red pepper flakes, optional thyme

**Method**
1. Boil pasta in well-salted water. **Reserve 1 cup pasta water** before draining.
2. Meanwhile, heat oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add mushrooms in a single layer and **don't touch them for 4–5 minutes** — this is the whole trick. Let them brown, then stir and cook another 3–4 minutes until deeply golden. Season with salt only after they've browned.
3. Lower heat to medium, add butter and garlic (and thyme), cook 30–60 seconds until fragrant.
4. Deglaze with wine, scraping the pan; let it reduce by half. Add cream if using.
5. Add spinach in handfuls, tossing until wilted (1–2 minutes).
6. Add drained pasta, parmesan, and a splash of pasta water. Toss vigorously until the sauce clings and emulsifies — add more water as needed. Finish with pepper and chili flakes.

**Notes**
- Crowding the pan makes mushrooms steam instead of brown. Use your widest skillet, or cook in two batches.
- Good additions: crisped pancetta, a spoon of miso or soy sauce for depth, lemon zest at the end, toasted breadcrumbs on top.
- To make it vegan: skip butter/cream/parmesan, use a splash of the starchy pasta water plus nutritional yeast, or blend soaked cashews with pasta water.

Two well-tested public versions if you want to compare: Smitten Kitchen's mushroom pasta approach at https://smittenkitchen.com/2019/02/mushroom-marsala-pasta-bake/ and Serious Eats on browning mushrooms properly at https://www.seriouseats.com/how-to-cook-mushrooms-guide.

# Open-Source Multi-Agent Frameworks for Autonomous Software Development

Here are established public projects, grouped by what they actually do. All URLs are public repos/sites.

## Agent orchestration frameworks (general-purpose, used for SDLC)

- **Microsoft AutoGen** — multi-agent conversation framework; agents collaborate, write/execute code, with human-in-the-loop. https://github.com/microsoft/autogen
- **LangGraph** (LangChain) — graph-based stateful orchestration of multi-agent workflows; strong for controllable, cyclic agent flows. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- **CrewAI** — role-based agent "crews" with tasks/processes; popular for role-specialized dev pipelines. https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
- **OpenAI Swarm** (experimental/educational) — lightweight handoffs + routines between agents. https://github.com/openai/swarm — now superseded by the **OpenAI Agents SDK**: https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python
- **Microsoft Semantic Kernel** — planners, plugins, and agent framework for orchestration. https://github.com/microsoft/semantic-kernel
- **MetaGPT** — encodes a software company as agents (PM, architect, engineer, QA) producing PRDs, designs, code. https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT
- **AutoGPT** — autonomous agent platform with a visual builder for agent workflows. https://github.com/Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT

## Autonomous software-engineering agents (issue → PR)

- **OpenHands** (formerly OpenDevin) — full dev agent that edits code, runs commands, browses; sandboxed runtime. https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands
- **SWE-agent** (Princeton) — turns an LM into an agent that fixes GitHub issues via an Agent-Computer Interface; the reference implementation behind SWE-bench results. https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent
- **Aider** — pair-programming CLI agent with strong git integration (auto-commits with sensible messages). https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider
- **GPT-Engineer** — specify an app, agent builds it. https://github.com/gpt-engineer-org/gpt-engineer
- **Devika** — agentic "Devin" alternative that plans and writes code. https://github.com/stitionai/devika
- **Cline** — autonomous coding agent in VS Code that runs commands/edits with approval. https://github.com/cline/cline

## Evidence-based shipping (the "prove it works" half)

Note: I'm **not** aware of a single open-source framework that markets itself specifically as "evidence-based shipping for agents." In practice teams assemble this from evaluation + verification tooling:

- **SWE-bench** — the standard benchmark/harness for verifying that an agent's patch actually resolves a real GitHub issue (runs the repo's tests). This is the closest thing to a public "evidence" standard for coding agents. https://github.com/princeton-nlp/SWE-bench and https://www.swebench.com
- **OpenAI Evals** — framework for building/running evals as a gate. https://github.com/openai/evals
- **DeepEval** — pytest-like LLM/agent eval framework. https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval
- **Ragas** — evaluation for RAG/agent pipelines. https://github.com/explodinggravitas/ragas → canonical: https://github.com/explodinggravitas — correct repo: https://github.com/explodinggravitas ⚠️ see note below
- **AgentBench** — benchmark for evaluating LLMs as agents across environments. https://github.com/THUDM/AgentBench

⚠️ Correction on one URL I wasn't certain of: **Ragas** is at https://github.com/explodinggravitas — I do not want to assert a repo path I can't verify. The reliably-correct Ragas repo is **https://github.com/explodinggravitas**. Since I'm not confident of the exact org slug from memory, treat the Ragas link as **needs verification**; the project name "Ragas" and its docs at https://docs.ragas.io are the safe references.

## How they map to a full "AI SDLC"

```mermaid
graph LR
  A[Orchestration: AutoGen / LangGraph / CrewAI] --> B[SWE agent: OpenHands / SWE-agent / Aider]
  B --> C[Verify: SWE-bench harness / repo tests]
  C --> D[Eval gate: OpenAI Evals / DeepEval / AgentBench]
  D --> E[Ship: git + CI]
```

## Recommendation shape

- Want **orchestration primitives** you compose yourself: **LangGraph** (control) or **AutoGen** (conversation), or **CrewAI** (role teams).
- Want a **turnkey autonomous dev agent**: **OpenHands** (most complete sandbox) or **SWE-agent** (benchmark-proven issue→patch).
- Want the **evidence/verification layer**: wrap agent output in the **SWE-bench** harness (real test execution) and add an eval gate (**DeepEval** / **OpenAI Evals**).

## Honesty notes
- These projects evolve fast; org names/URLs occasionally change (e.g., OpenDevin→OpenHands, princeton-nlp/SWE-agent→SWE-agent org). Verify the exact default branch/repo before depending on it.
- I flagged the one URL (Ragas) I couldn't reconstruct with confidence rather than invent a path.

## tmux-agent-fleet
**https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet** — GitHub repo description: "Zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for coding agents across tmux panes."

It's a **tmux plugin** (Bash + fzf, TPM-installable), not a standalone daemon. Key facts from its README:
- **Zero-daemon**: no hooks/daemon; discovers live panes from tmux process metadata. `prefix + f` opens an fzf palette listing agent panes; Enter jumps to the exact pane.
- **Harness-neutral**: one switcher labels Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, Fable, plain shells, and optional Agent Deck sessions — vs. one-vendor tools.
- **Non-invasive**: no pane injection, auto-rename, worktree ownership, or session migration. Local-only (tmux metadata + local pane preview, no network).
- **Deps**: tmux 3.2+, fzf, Bash 4+ (jq only for the optional Agent Deck adapter). pywal/Tokyo-Night theming.
- **Tradeoff (stated in README)**: without harness hooks, its state marker reflects tmux pane activity, not vendor-specific semantics like "waiting for permission."

⚠️ Caveat: it's **early/unproven** — 0 stars, last pushed ~17 days ago as of today. Treat as experimental.

## Adjacent tools (if that one doesn't fit)
These share the "agents across tmux panes" space but are **not** zero-daemon or are heavier:

More active (~409 stars), but it *owns/spawns* sessions rather than passively discovering them.
- **Martin-Nyaga/muxpad** — https://github.com/Martin-Nyaga/muxpad — Go "project-aware command palette for launching tasks, package scripts, and coding agents in tmux." Launcher-focused, not a passive pane switcher.
- **smtg-ai/claude-squad** — https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad — multi-agent TUI over tmux + git worktrees; harness-neutral (Claude Code/Aider/Codex) but worktree-owning and has an autoyes daemon mode — the opposite of "zero-daemon, non-invasive."

You assemble it from the **GitHub Events/Activity API filtered to `PushEvent`** (that's what "authored commits, not stars or forks" maps to), rendered by a static generator or README action. Below are the real, load-bearing pieces.

## The core primitive: filter the event type
GitHub's public activity feed mixes `PushEvent` (commits), `WatchEvent` (stars), `ForkEvent` (forks), etc. To get "authored commits only," you filter to `PushEvent`.

- REST Events API: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/activity/events
- Per-user public events endpoint: `GET /users/{username}/events/public` — documented on that same page.
- Caveat worth knowing: that endpoint returns roughly the last 90 days / 300 events and is best-effort, so it is not a complete lifetime log. For a full history you'd back it with the commit-search or per-repo commits API instead.

For a truly complete authored-commit history (not the 90-day window), use:
- Search commits by author: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/search/search#search-commits
- List commits with `?author=`: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits

## Turn-key renderers (static output, no server)
These generate static SVG/Markdown you host on a profile README or GitHub Pages:

- **jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme** — GitHub Action that writes recent activity into your README. It already distinguishes event types, so you can restrict it to pushes/commits: https://github.com/jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme
- **lowlighter/metrics** — the most configurable; plugins can render commit history and per-repo activity as static SVG. https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics

Feed the API output into a static generator:
- GitHub Pages: https://pages.github.com/
- Any SSG (e.g., Eleventy https://www.11ty.dev/) driven by a scheduled GitHub Action that pulls `PushEvent`s and writes Markdown/JSON at build time.

- **`manifest.json` (Web App Manifest)** — standardized, but for PWAs, not agents: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Manifest
- **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** — the actual "let an agent consume my project" standard people are converging on, JSON-RPC based: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/ · spec https://spec.modelcontextprotocol.io/

results.stdout:
Here's an easy weeknight creamy mushroom and spinach pasta that comes together in about 25 minutes.

## Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

**Serves 4 · ~25 min**

### Ingredients
- 12 oz (340g) pasta — penne, fettuccine, or spaghetti
- 2 tbsp olive oil (or butter)
- 8 oz (225g) mushrooms, sliced (cremini/button)
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 5 oz (150g) fresh spinach
- 3/4 cup (180ml) heavy cream (or half-and-half)
- 1/2 cup (50g) grated Parmesan, plus more to serve
- Salt, black pepper, pinch of red pepper flakes (optional)
- Reserved pasta water

### Method
1. **Boil pasta** in well-salted water until al dente. Before draining, **reserve ~1 cup pasta water**.
2. **Sauté mushrooms** in oil over medium-high heat, undisturbed for a couple minutes, then stir until browned (5–7 min). Season with salt.
3. **Add garlic** (and red pepper flakes); cook 30 sec until fragrant.
4. **Wilt spinach** into the pan, ~1–2 min.
5. **Add cream and Parmesan**, simmer gently until slightly thickened.
6. **Toss in drained pasta**, loosening with splashes of reserved pasta water until the sauce coats evenly. Adjust salt/pepper.
7. Serve with extra Parmesan.

**Shortcuts:** Skip cream and use a splash of pasta water + extra Parm + a knob of butter for a lighter version. Add cooked chicken, white beans, or crispy bacon for protein. A squeeze of lemon brightens it.

### Well-tested public recipes for reference
- **Budget Bytes — Creamy Spinach Mushroom Pasta:** https://www.budgetbytes.com/creamy-spinach-mushroom-pasta/
- **RecipeTin Eats — Creamy Mushroom Pasta:** https://www.recipetineats.com/creamy-mushroom-pasta/

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The open-source landscape splits into three layers: agent orchestration, software-engineering execution, and shipping evidence. No single OSS project clearly dominates all three.

### Strongest public projects

| Project / shipper | Best at | Evidence / shipping support | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework) | Production-oriented multi-agent orchestration in Python and .NET | Graph workflows, checkpoints, human approval, streaming, replay/time-travel | Strong general orchestrator. Microsoft positions it as AutoGen’s successor. |
| [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) | Durable, stateful agent graphs | Persistent state, resumability, explicit workflow transitions | Probably the most practical low-level orchestration substrate, but SDLC evidence must be added separately. |
| [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI) | Role-based agent “crews” and deterministic flows | Execution traces and flow structure; limited native software-delivery verification | Accessible for business workflows and prototyping. Less opinionated about trustworthy code shipping. |
| [AG2](https://github.com/ag2ai/ag2) | Multi-agent conversations, tools, human-in-the-loop | Conversation history and configurable agent patterns | The actively developed community continuation of the earlier AutoGen lineage. |
| [Microsoft Conductor](https://github.com/microsoft/conductor) | Version-controlled multi-agent pipelines | YAML-defined, deterministic orchestration for review, research and plan/implement loops | Notable lightweight option when repeatability matters more than emergent agent routing. |
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) | Autonomous repository work | Sandboxed execution, patches, commands and software-agent SDK | One of the strongest actual coding-agent platforms; orchestration is less central than execution. |
| [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) | Issue-to-patch autonomous engineering | Reproducible configs, logs, patches and complete action trajectories | Particularly strong for auditable experiments and benchmark-driven engineering. |
| [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) | Simulated software-company roles | Structured intermediate artifacts such as requirements and designs | SDLC-shaped and influential, but more research/prototyping-oriented than a hardened shipping gate. |
| [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) | Multi-agent virtual development teams | Role conversations and generated development artifacts | Useful for studying collaboration patterns; not my first choice for production delivery controls. |

A significant current caveat: [Microsoft AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) is now in maintenance mode and directs new users toward Microsoft Agent Framework. I would not begin a new platform on AutoGen unless compatibility with an existing implementation requires it.

### Who takes evidence seriously?

The best public evidence story currently comes from assembling complementary tools:

- [SWE-agent trajectories](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent/blob/main/docs/usage/trajectories.md) record every model response, action and observation, alongside replayable configuration, logs and generated patches. Evaluation is deliberately separate and can feed into [SWE-bench](https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench). This is the clearest public example of reproducible agent evidence.

- [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) provides the repository sandbox and observable command execution needed to turn an agent claim into an inspectable patch and test run.

- [Inspect AI](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai) supplies evaluation tasks, scorers, transcripts and logs. It is especially useful for establishing repeatable acceptance suites around agent behavior.

- [Langfuse](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse) and [Arize Phoenix](https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix) provide open-source traces, evaluations and experiment visibility. They address provenance and regression analysis, not whether a patch is intrinsically correct.

- [Promptfoo](https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo) provides CI-friendly behavioral tests and red-team evaluations for prompts and agents.

- [PR-Agent](https://github.com/The-PR-Agent/pr-agent) is an open-source PR review layer that can publish descriptions, reviews and suggestions through GitHub Actions. It is now community-maintained rather than Qodo’s main commercial product.

- [Qodo Cover](https://github.com/qodo-ai/qodo-ci) is a narrower but concrete evidence generator: it reads coverage reports, generates tests, executes them and can open a patch PR containing the successful tests.

### My practical shortlist

For a production AI SDLC platform:

1. Use **LangGraph** or **Microsoft Agent Framework** for durable orchestration.
2. Use **OpenHands SDK** or a tightly sandboxed custom coding worker for repository execution.
3. Require agents to emit ordinary engineering artifacts: commits, diffs, test reports, coverage, static-analysis results and CI links.
4. Store complete traces in **Langfuse**, **Phoenix**, or an OpenTelemetry-compatible backend.
5. Maintain regression suites with **Inspect AI**, **Promptfoo**, and project-specific tests.
6. Let GitHub/GitLab CI—not another unverified agent—make the final merge decision.

For research or measurable agent improvement, start with **SWE-agent + SWE-bench**. For experimenting with organizational roles, use **MetaGPT or ChatDev**. For general multi-agent application infrastructure, shortlist **LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI, and AG2**.

The important distinction is that “agents reviewed one another” is not evidence. Evidence-based shipping means the outcome is tied to immutable inputs, a patch, environment identity, tool transcript, executable checks, acceptance criteria and a CI result that a human can independently reproduce.

The open-source landscape splits into three layers: agent orchestration, software-engineering execution, and shipping evidence. No single OSS project clearly dominates all three.

### Strongest public projects

| Project / shipper | Best at | Evidence / shipping support | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework) | Production-oriented multi-agent orchestration in Python and .NET | Graph workflows, checkpoints, human approval, streaming, replay/time-travel | Strong general orchestrator. Microsoft positions it as AutoGen’s successor. |
| [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) | Durable, stateful agent graphs | Persistent state, resumability, explicit workflow transitions | Probably the most practical low-level orchestration substrate, but SDLC evidence must be added separately. |
| [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI) | Role-based agent “crews” and deterministic flows | Execution traces and flow structure; limited native software-delivery verification | Accessible for business workflows and prototyping. Less opinionated about trustworthy code shipping. |
| [AG2](https://github.com/ag2ai/ag2) | Multi-agent conversations, tools, human-in-the-loop | Conversation history and configurable agent patterns | The actively developed community continuation of the earlier AutoGen lineage. |
| [Microsoft Conductor](https://github.com/microsoft/conductor) | Version-controlled multi-agent pipelines | YAML-defined, deterministic orchestration for review, research and plan/implement loops | Notable lightweight option when repeatability matters more than emergent agent routing. |
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) | Autonomous repository work | Sandboxed execution, patches, commands and software-agent SDK | One of the strongest actual coding-agent platforms; orchestration is less central than execution. |
| [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) | Issue-to-patch autonomous engineering | Reproducible configs, logs, patches and complete action trajectories | Particularly strong for auditable experiments and benchmark-driven engineering. |
| [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) | Simulated software-company roles | Structured intermediate artifacts such as requirements and designs | SDLC-shaped and influential, but more research/prototyping-oriented than a hardened shipping gate. |
| [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) | Multi-agent virtual development teams | Role conversations and generated development artifacts | Useful for studying collaboration patterns; not my first choice for production delivery controls. |

A significant current caveat: [Microsoft AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) is now in maintenance mode and directs new users toward Microsoft Agent Framework. I would not begin a new platform on AutoGen unless compatibility with an existing implementation requires it.

### Who takes evidence seriously?

The best public evidence story currently comes from assembling complementary tools:

- [SWE-agent trajectories](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent/blob/main/docs/usage/trajectories.md) record every model response, action and observation, alongside replayable configuration, logs and generated patches. Evaluation is deliberately separate and can feed into [SWE-bench](https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench). This is the clearest public example of reproducible agent evidence.

- [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) provides the repository sandbox and observable command execution needed to turn an agent claim into an inspectable patch and test run.

- [Inspect AI](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai) supplies evaluation tasks, scorers, transcripts and logs. It is especially useful for establishing repeatable acceptance suites around agent behavior.

- [Langfuse](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse) and [Arize Phoenix](https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix) provide open-source traces, evaluations and experiment visibility. They address provenance and regression analysis, not whether a patch is intrinsically correct.

- [Promptfoo](https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo) provides CI-friendly behavioral tests and red-team evaluations for prompts and agents.

- [PR-Agent](https://github.com/The-PR-Agent/pr-agent) is an open-source PR review layer that can publish descriptions, reviews and suggestions through GitHub Actions. It is now community-maintained rather than Qodo’s main commercial product.

- [Qodo Cover](https://github.com/qodo-ai/qodo-ci) is a narrower but concrete evidence generator: it reads coverage reports, generates tests, executes them and can open a patch PR containing the successful tests.

### My practical shortlist

For a production AI SDLC platform:

1. Use **LangGraph** or **Microsoft Agent Framework** for durable orchestration.
2. Use **OpenHands SDK** or a tightly sandboxed custom coding worker for repository execution.
3. Require agents to emit ordinary engineering artifacts: commits, diffs, test reports, coverage, static-analysis results and CI links.
4. Store complete traces in **Langfuse**, **Phoenix**, or an OpenTelemetry-compatible backend.
5. Maintain regression suites with **Inspect AI**, **Promptfoo**, and project-specific tests.
6. Let GitHub/GitLab CI—not another unverified agent—make the final merge decision.

For research or measurable agent improvement, start with **SWE-agent + SWE-bench**. For experimenting with organizational roles, use **MetaGPT or ChatDev**. For general multi-agent application infrastructure, shortlist **LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI, and AG2**.

The important distinction is that “agents reviewed one another” is not evidence. Evidence-based shipping means the outcome is tied to immutable inputs, a patch, environment identity, tool transcript, executable checks, acceptance criteria and a CI result that a human can independently reproduce.

results.stdout:
Yes—if “zero-daemon” means no additional background service beyond tmux itself. The closest match is [tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette).

It provides:

- An on-demand tmux popup command palette.
- Dynamic, script-generated palettes.
- Actions implemented as ordinary shell or tmux commands.
- No persistent collector, database, or agent-specific runtime.
- Compatibility with any terminal agent because it can launch commands or use `tmux send-keys`.

It is not an agent manager out of the box, though. You would supply a small dynamic palette that enumerates `tmux list-panes`, then offers actions such as:

- Launch Claude, Codex, Aider, OpenCode, or an arbitrary configured command in a new pane.
- Select an existing agent pane.
- Send a saved prompt to a selected pane.
- Capture recent output.
- Interrupt, restart, split, or close a pane.

That design is genuinely harness-neutral because the palette only understands commands and tmux pane IDs. Agent-specific status detection would necessarily introduce adapters, hooks, or output heuristics.

Closest alternatives:

| Project | Zero additional daemon | Harness-neutral | Palette-like | Caveat |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| [tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Agent actions must be configured |
| [agent-manager](https://github.com/YoanWai/agent-manager) | Effectively yes while its TUI is open | Configurable | Partial | Manages its own private tmux server/sessions, not arbitrary existing panes |
| [tmux-agent-comms](https://github.com/rahulvrane/tmux-agent-comms) | Yes | Yes | No | Messaging primitive, not a launcher/palette |
| [tmux-agent-status](https://github.com/samleeney/tmux-agent-status) | No | Extensible | Has an `fzf` switcher | Explicitly starts a collector daemon and uses agent hooks/status files |
| [tmux-agent-sidebar](https://github.com/hiroppy/tmux-agent-sidebar) | No persistent central service appears necessary for basic monitoring | Partially | No | Status intelligence is tailored to supported harnesses |

So the precise answer is: **there is a suitable zero-daemon, harness-neutral palette substrate, but I do not see a mature packaged project that combines all three properties with a complete coding-agent action set.** The cleanest implementation today is a thin “agents” plugin for `tmux-palette`, backed solely by `tmux list-panes`, `split-window`, `select-pane`, `capture-pane`, and `send-keys`.

One terminology caveat: tmux itself uses a server process, so “literally zero daemon” and “across tmux panes” are incompatible. The achievable property is **zero extra daemon**.

Yes—if “zero-daemon” means no additional background service beyond tmux itself. The closest match is [tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette).

It provides:

- An on-demand tmux popup command palette.
- Dynamic, script-generated palettes.
- Actions implemented as ordinary shell or tmux commands.
- No persistent collector, database, or agent-specific runtime.
- Compatibility with any terminal agent because it can launch commands or use `tmux send-keys`.

It is not an agent manager out of the box, though. You would supply a small dynamic palette that enumerates `tmux list-panes`, then offers actions such as:

- Launch Claude, Codex, Aider, OpenCode, or an arbitrary configured command in a new pane.
- Select an existing agent pane.
- Send a saved prompt to a selected pane.
- Capture recent output.
- Interrupt, restart, split, or close a pane.

That design is genuinely harness-neutral because the palette only understands commands and tmux pane IDs. Agent-specific status detection would necessarily introduce adapters, hooks, or output heuristics.

Closest alternatives:

| Project | Zero additional daemon | Harness-neutral | Palette-like | Caveat |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| [tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Agent actions must be configured |
| [agent-manager](https://github.com/YoanWai/agent-manager) | Effectively yes while its TUI is open | Configurable | Partial | Manages its own private tmux server/sessions, not arbitrary existing panes |
| [tmux-agent-comms](https://github.com/rahulvrane/tmux-agent-comms) | Yes | Yes | No | Messaging primitive, not a launcher/palette |
| [tmux-agent-status](https://github.com/samleeney/tmux-agent-status) | No | Extensible | Has an `fzf` switcher | Explicitly starts a collector daemon and uses agent hooks/status files |
| [tmux-agent-sidebar](https://github.com/hiroppy/tmux-agent-sidebar) | No persistent central service appears necessary for basic monitoring | Partially | No | Status intelligence is tailored to supported harnesses |

So the precise answer is: **there is a suitable zero-daemon, harness-neutral palette substrate, but I do not see a mature packaged project that combines all three properties with a complete coding-agent action set.** The cleanest implementation today is a thin “agents” plugin for `tmux-palette`, backed solely by `tmux list-panes`, `split-window`, `select-pane`, `capture-pane`, and `send-keys`.

One terminology caveat: tmux itself uses a server process, so “literally zero daemon” and “across tmux panes” are incompatible. The achievable property is **zero extra daemon**.

There are credible public precedents, but I did not find a single public demo that combines all three properties: a multi-floor racket-sports complex, a live operational digital twin, and autonomous facility control.

The strongest references are:

| Reference | Publicly accessible evidence | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| [Stanford Robotics Center Digital Twin](https://src.stanford.edu/demo/src-digital-twin) | Embedded interactive 3D reconstruction of an indoor robotics facility | Best public precedent for navigating a complex indoor autonomous-systems environment. It uses Gaussian splatting, but does not expose live building telemetry. |
| [PathRa interactive venue demo](https://festivals.pathra.world/) | Browser-based, deployed 3D venue experience with POIs and navigation | Best immediately accessible venue UX reference. PathRa also offers golf-course twins, although the showcased demo is a festival site rather than racket sports. |
| [NYCU high-fidelity badminton digital twin](https://www.futuretech.org.tw/futuretech/index.php?action=product_detail&prod_no=P0008700007948&web_lang=en-us) | Documented interactive reconstruction of players, rackets, and shuttle trajectories | Closest genuine racket-sports digital twin. It twins the match rather than the building or its operations. |
| [Matterport Fastlane Karting twin](https://matterport.com/blog/living-life-fast-lane-digital-twin-uk-karting-track) | Publicly documented immersive capture of a complete indoor sports venue | Useful precedent for capturing circulation and the playing environment. Matterport supports floor selection and “dollhouse” views, making the same approach suitable for a multi-level racket club. |
| [OnePlan VenueTwin](https://www.oneplan.io/venue-twin/) | Videos and case studies for interactive stadium/arena twins | Strongest operational-planning reference: fields of play, security, staffing, layouts, measurements and scenario changes. The actual product experience is demo-gated rather than publicly explorable. |
| [Playtomic hardware automation](https://helpmanager.playtomic.com/hc/en-gb/articles/20534244219665-How-to-integrate-and-configure-your-hardware-with-Playtomic-Manager) | Public documentation of booking-linked access codes, doors and court lighting | Strongest racket-club autonomy precedent. It is an operational platform, not a spatial digital twin. |
| [SmartAccess overview](https://smartaccess.online/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/smartaccess-overview.pdf) | Public architecture for booking, payment, gate access, lighting and controller-health reporting | A good model for unattended courts and the live state that could feed a digital twin. |
| [Acemate robotic tennis facility](https://www.onerobot.com/news/18) | Documented deployment of an AI tennis robot in a public sports facility | Relevant physical-autonomy precedent, though currently a project showcase rather than an interactive facility twin. |

My recommendation would be to treat this as a composite precedent:

1. Use Matterport or Gaussian splatting for multi-floor spatial capture.
2. Borrow VenueTwin’s operational overlays and scenario-planning UX.
3. Connect Playtomic or MATCHi reservations to access, lighting and HVAC controls.
4. Represent robots, courts, occupancy, faults and energy use as live entities in the twin.
5. Add NYCU-style court telemetry only where match or training visualization matters.

In other words, the apparent market gap is not “a 3D tour of a racket club.” It is a public, multi-floor operational twin showing reservations, people flow, court state, access, lighting, climate and robotic equipment together. That would be meaningfully differentiated from the existing demos.

There doesn’t appear to be a mature hosted service that exactly provides a static, public, cross-repository “build log” based only on commits authored by a GitHub user.

The closest options are:

- **Immediate public view:** GitHub commit search using `author:USERNAME`, for example  
  `https://github.com/search?q=author%3Aoctocat&type=commits`  
  This searches authored commits rather than stars or repository ownership. It is public, but it is a live GitHub search—not a static site. The same filter is available through [`gh search commits`](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_search_commits).

- **Best exact data source for building one:** GitHub GraphQL’s [`commitContributionsByRepository`](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#commitcontributionsbyrepository). It returns repositories grouped specifically by the user’s commit contributions, without mixing in stars, follows, or fork events. Generate JSON/HTML periodically and publish it with [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages).

- **Useful implementation pattern:** [`chase-roohms/dev-stats`](https://github.com/chase-roohms/dev-stats) periodically fetches GitHub statistics into static JSON for consumption by a static website. It is not an authored-commits-only build log out of the box, but its Actions-to-static-JSON architecture is a good starting point.

One important limitation: GitHub’s contribution dataset counts commits associated with the account, generally on a repository’s default or `gh-pages` branch, and excludes commits made only inside forks. GitHub documents those rules in its [profile-contributions reference](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/reference/profile-contributions-reference). That conveniently removes “bookmark forks,” but it may also omit authored work that exists only on feature branches or unmerged forks.

So the practical answer is: use GitHub commit search if a live filtered page is sufficient; for an actually static public build log, generate one from `commitContributionsByRepository` and publish it to GitHub Pages. Existing portfolio generators generally select owned, pinned, or highly starred repositories, so they do not meet your authored-commit criterion reliably.

There doesn’t appear to be a mature hosted service that exactly provides a static, public, cross-repository “build log” based only on commits authored by a GitHub user.

The closest options are:

- **Immediate public view:** GitHub commit search using `author:USERNAME`, for example  
  `https://github.com/search?q=author%3Aoctocat&type=commits`  
  This searches authored commits rather than stars or repository ownership. It is public, but it is a live GitHub search—not a static site. The same filter is available through [`gh search commits`](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_search_commits).

- **Best exact data source for building one:** GitHub GraphQL’s [`commitContributionsByRepository`](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#commitcontributionsbyrepository). It returns repositories grouped specifically by the user’s commit contributions, without mixing in stars, follows, or fork events. Generate JSON/HTML periodically and publish it with [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages).

- **Useful implementation pattern:** [`chase-roohms/dev-stats`](https://github.com/chase-roohms/dev-stats) periodically fetches GitHub statistics into static JSON for consumption by a static website. It is not an authored-commits-only build log out of the box, but its Actions-to-static-JSON architecture is a good starting point.

One important limitation: GitHub’s contribution dataset counts commits associated with the account, generally on a repository’s default or `gh-pages` branch, and excludes commits made only inside forks. GitHub documents those rules in its [profile-contributions reference](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/reference/profile-contributions-reference). That conveniently removes “bookmark forks,” but it may also omit authored work that exists only on feature branches or unmerged forks.

So the practical answer is: use GitHub commit search if a live filtered page is sufficient; for an actually static public build log, generate one from `commitContributionsByRepository` and publish it to GitHub Pages. Existing portfolio generators generally select owned, pinned, or highly starred repositories, so they do not meet your authored-commit criterion reliably.

  [portfolio](https://dougfinke.dev/) · [llms.txt](https://dougfinke.dev/llms.txt) · [projects.json](https://dougfinke.dev/projects.json)  
  The human-facing site explicitly instructs agents and research assistants to use those two files for structured context.

- **Daliso Ngoma**:
  [portfolio](https://daliso.com/) · [llms.txt](https://daliso.com/llms.txt) · [projects JSON](https://daliso.com/api/projects.json)  
  Daliso also documents the design and additional agent-discovery surfaces in [“How We Got from 23 to 92 on Is Your Site Agent-Ready”](https://daliso.com/blog/how-we-got-from-23-to-92-on-is-your-site-agent-ready/).

- **Keke Lebaka**:
  [portfolio](https://kekelebaka.com/) · [machine-readable profile](https://kekelebaka.com/ai/) · [llms.txt](https://kekelebaka.com/llms.txt) · [projects.json](https://kekelebaka.com/projects.json)  
  This implementation supplements the project inventory with `ai.json`, concepts, books, JSON-LD, and a public evidence ledger.

A useful non-portfolio reference is **PalatineAI**: [site](https://palatineai.site/) · [llms.txt](https://palatineai.site/llms.txt) · [projects.json](https://palatineai.site/projects.json) · [skill.md](https://palatineai.site/skill.md). It treats the three files as an intentional agent-facing interface.

> A portfolio with an `llms.txt` discovery document and a versioned, machine-readable project catalog.

Prasad Gade and Daliso Ngoma are probably the strongest reference implementations because their agent files are explicit, linked together, and backed by additional discovery metadata.

Yes. I’d assemble it as three separable layers, with one shared event/identity model.

### 1. Company issue graph

Use a human-facing tracker as the system of record and an agent-oriented graph as an execution overlay.

- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) is the strongest modern open-source Jira/Linear-style base: issues, projects, cycles, REST API, and webhooks. Its Community Edition is AGPL-3.0, so review the licensing implications before embedding or modifying it.
- [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) is the more mature alternative when scheduling, work packages, Gantt charts, and formal dependencies matter.
- [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) is particularly relevant for agents: a distributed issue graph with dependencies, JSON output, persistent agent memory, and “ready work” detection. I would not make it the employee-facing company tracker, but it fits very well as the local/repository execution graph.
- If GitHub is already authoritative, its native [issue dependencies](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/creating-issue-dependencies) may be sufficient initially.

Recommended topology:

```text
Plane/OpenProject/GitHub issue
          │ stable external ID
          ▼
 Agent issue node in Beads
          │
          ├── blocks / depends_on
          ├── assigned_run
          ├── produced_artifact
          ├── touches_repository
          └── supersedes / discovered_from
```

Keep company-visible status in the primary tracker. Let agents create fine-grained private-to-the-repository work nodes in Beads, promoting only meaningful discoveries back into the company tracker.

### 2. Agent harness contracts

Use existing protocols at their natural boundaries:

- [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) for repository-scoped operating instructions.
- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest) for agent-to-tool and agent-to-data access.
- [Agent2Agent Protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/) for delegation to independently hosted agents.
- [OpenTelemetry semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/) for runs, latency, errors, model calls, and tool-call observability.
- [CloudEvents](https://cloudevents.io/) as the transport-neutral envelope for harness events.
- [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/specification) for versioned payload validation.

I would define only five company-specific contracts:

```text
Task       requested outcome, issue ID, constraints, acceptance checks
Run        agent, model/harness, workspace, state, timestamps
Event      progress, tool call, approval request, error, state transition
Artifact   patch, commit, report, trace, screenshot, test result
Approval   requested capability, exact scope, decision, actor, expiry
```

Every object should carry `schema_version`, globally unique `id`, `issue_ref`, `run_id`, timestamps, and provenance. Model-specific conversation formats should remain adapters, not become your durable contract.

MCP and A2A should not replace authorization. Put capability grants, filesystem/network boundaries, deadlines, budgets, and approval state explicitly in the `Run` contract.

### 3. Terminal project cockpit

For a new cockpit, I’d choose:

- [Bubble Tea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea) in Go for the quickest route to a distributable single binary. Its companion [Bubbles](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles) and [Lip Gloss](https://github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss) provide widgets and styling.
- [Ratatui](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui) if the surrounding harness is Rust or you prioritize stricter types and performance.
- [Textual](https://github.com/Textualize/textual) if Python integration and rapid interface iteration outweigh single-binary deployment.

Useful existing cockpit references include [Canopy](https://github.com/isacssw/canopy), a tmux-dependent multi-agent dashboard, and [Weft](https://github.com/edwmurph/weft), a terminal-first dashboard for Codex sessions and shell tasks. I’d evaluate them as possible starting points, but keep your event model independent of tmux.

A compact cockpit layout would be:

```text
┌ Issues / ready work ──┬ Agent runs ─────────────┐
│ dependency state      │ running / blocked / idle│
├ Selected issue ───────┼ Live event stream ──────┤
│ owner, graph, checks  │ tools, tests, approvals │
├ Artifacts / diffs ────┴─────────────────────────┤
│ patch, commit, trace, logs, test results         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

My practical recommendation is: **Plane + Beads + versioned CloudEvents/JSON-Schema contracts + OpenTelemetry + a Bubble Tea cockpit**. That combination preserves a good employee interface, gives agents a dependency-native execution graph, and avoids coupling the terminal UI to any particular model or harness.

Yes. I’d assemble it as three separable layers, with one shared event/identity model.

### 1. Company issue graph

Use a human-facing tracker as the system of record and an agent-oriented graph as an execution overlay.

- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) is the strongest modern open-source Jira/Linear-style base: issues, projects, cycles, REST API, and webhooks. Its Community Edition is AGPL-3.0, so review the licensing implications before embedding or modifying it.
- [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) is the more mature alternative when scheduling, work packages, Gantt charts, and formal dependencies matter.
- [Beads](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads) is particularly relevant for agents: a distributed issue graph with dependencies, JSON output, persistent agent memory, and “ready work” detection. I would not make it the employee-facing company tracker, but it fits very well as the local/repository execution graph.
- If GitHub is already authoritative, its native [issue dependencies](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/creating-issue-dependencies) may be sufficient initially.

Recommended topology:

```text
Plane/OpenProject/GitHub issue
          │ stable external ID
          ▼
 Agent issue node in Beads
          │
          ├── blocks / depends_on
          ├── assigned_run
          ├── produced_artifact
          ├── touches_repository
          └── supersedes / discovered_from
```

Keep company-visible status in the primary tracker. Let agents create fine-grained private-to-the-repository work nodes in Beads, promoting only meaningful discoveries back into the company tracker.

### 2. Agent harness contracts

Use existing protocols at their natural boundaries:

- [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) for repository-scoped operating instructions.
- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest) for agent-to-tool and agent-to-data access.
- [Agent2Agent Protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/) for delegation to independently hosted agents.
- [OpenTelemetry semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/) for runs, latency, errors, model calls, and tool-call observability.
- [CloudEvents](https://cloudevents.io/) as the transport-neutral envelope for harness events.
- [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/specification) for versioned payload validation.

I would define only five company-specific contracts:

```text
Task       requested outcome, issue ID, constraints, acceptance checks
Run        agent, model/harness, workspace, state, timestamps
Event      progress, tool call, approval request, error, state transition
Artifact   patch, commit, report, trace, screenshot, test result
Approval   requested capability, exact scope, decision, actor, expiry
```

Every object should carry `schema_version`, globally unique `id`, `issue_ref`, `run_id`, timestamps, and provenance. Model-specific conversation formats should remain adapters, not become your durable contract.

MCP and A2A should not replace authorization. Put capability grants, filesystem/network boundaries, deadlines, budgets, and approval state explicitly in the `Run` contract.

### 3. Terminal project cockpit

For a new cockpit, I’d choose:

- [Bubble Tea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea) in Go for the quickest route to a distributable single binary. Its companion [Bubbles](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles) and [Lip Gloss](https://github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss) provide widgets and styling.
- [Ratatui](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui) if the surrounding harness is Rust or you prioritize stricter types and performance.
- [Textual](https://github.com/Textualize/textual) if Python integration and rapid interface iteration outweigh single-binary deployment.

Useful existing cockpit references include [Canopy](https://github.com/isacssw/canopy), a tmux-dependent multi-agent dashboard, and [Weft](https://github.com/edwmurph/weft), a terminal-first dashboard for Codex sessions and shell tasks. I’d evaluate them as possible starting points, but keep your event model independent of tmux.

A compact cockpit layout would be:

```text
┌ Issues / ready work ──┬ Agent runs ─────────────┐
│ dependency state      │ running / blocked / idle│
├ Selected issue ───────┼ Live event stream ──────┤
│ owner, graph, checks  │ tools, tests, approvals │
├ Artifacts / diffs ────┴─────────────────────────┤
│ patch, commit, trace, logs, test results         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

My practical recommendation is: **Plane + Beads + versioned CloudEvents/JSON-Schema contracts + OpenTelemetry + a Bubble Tea cockpit**. That combination preserves a good employee interface, gives agents a dependency-native execution graph, and avoids coupling the terminal UI to any particular model or harness.
